extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (OED, respondents, administrative law judges)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures governing motions for reconsideration of USPTO disciplinary initial decisions, the aggravating/mitigating factors to be weighed for sanctions, and the terms and revocation process for probation and suspension in USPTO disciplinary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for reconsideration of an initial decision
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations authorize the USPTO Director to grant a request for reconsideration or modification of the Director's final order if the request is based on newly discovered evidence or error of law or fact. 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court adopts and applies the same standard generally applied in federal courts (citing Arthur v. King and Harrington v. City of Chicago) when reviewing a motion to reconsider an initial decision. A motion that merely re-argues previously considered points without new evidence or identified errors of law/fact is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to consider 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) factors and ABA Standards when imposing sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court must consider the factors set forth in 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) and the American Bar Association's Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions when determining an appropriate sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions should be based on the enumerated factors and the entire record of the proceeding. A sanction cannot properly be imposed (or increased on reconsideration) without analysis under § 11.54(b). The passage of time (e.g., length of a state suspension) alone is not a proper basis for increasing a sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor: pattern of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent exhibited a pattern of misconduct by repeatedly ignoring requests for information made by the State Bar of Georgia and the OED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court identified this as an aggravating factor after reviewing the record; pattern of repeated noncooperation or ignoring inquiries supports a more severe sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor: bad-faith obstruction (including failure to appear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad-faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding — alleged to include failing to appear for the hearing — is a potential aggravating factor under the ABA Standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to appear is not automatically aggravating. It is aggravating only if it caused delay or disruption of proceedings, or violated a subpoena or court order. Mere absence that results in waiver of a hearing (and does not disrupt the process) may not warrant a harsher sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor: false statement to the OED
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a false statement submitted to the OED during the disciplinary process is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court found the respondent's false statement to be an aggravating factor supporting a more severe sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor: refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing (taking responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to acknowledge the wrongful nature of conduct or failure to take responsibility can be an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor must be supported by evidence that the respondent refused to accept responsibility. Where record evidence shows cooperation or reinstatement based on sufficient cooperation, the Court may find this factor not present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on relying on other orders or passage-of-time when setting sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A sanction based solely on another forum's suspension length or the passage of time it took to comply is not persuasive; the USPTO must apply its own regulatory factors in § 11.54(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final Orders resulting from settlement agreements that do not analyze § 11.54(b) factors (e.g., a settlement-based six-month suspension) are not persuasive precedent for imposing a sanction absent the required analysis. The severity of sanction should be tied to the specific § 11.54(b) factors, not simply mirror state discipline durations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation and suspension revocation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms clarifying suspension and probation: a specified initial suspension period, a probationary period beginning upon OED-granted reinstatement (here, 275 days), and mechanisms by which the OED may seek additional suspension if probation conditions are violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: (a) OED may issue an Order to Show Cause if it believes the respondent violated probation or disciplinary rules; (b) OED must send the Order to the respondent's last address of record and grant 15 days to respond; (c) after the response period, OED may deliver the Order to Show Cause, respondent's response, and evidence to the USPTO Director and request immediate additional suspension for up to the stated number of days (275 in this order); (d) if the USPTO Director enters such an order, judicial review does not stay the Director's suspension. Probation begins upon the OED Director granting a reinstatement petition under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of reciprocal-discipline procedures vs. independent disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 allows the USPTO Director to impose reciprocal sanctions when a respondent is sanctioned by a state bar, but proceedings brought under 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.32–11.57 are independent disciplinary proceedings and must follow those procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a matter is brought as an independent disciplinary proceeding, the Court must follow §§ 11.32–11.57 procedures (including § 11.54(b) analysis) rather than treating it as a reciprocal-discipline case under § 11.24. The existence of state-bar discipline may inform but does not automatically dictate USPTO sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing process rule on waiver for nonappearance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a respondent fails to appear at the hearing after notice, the Court may deem the respondent to have waived the right to a hearing and may proceed in his absence. 37 C.F.R. § 11.44(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent has a due-process right to appear but no duty to travel to D.C. or to file a response to every motion. Waiver of the right to submit a post-hearing brief or to appear is not itself necessarily an aggravating factor if it did not prejudice or disrupt the proceedings.
